bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Only Indian supplier with approved products for HVDC transformers, and approved for all classes of power transformers - a position reinforced during the year by an award of 37 HVDC transformers, the first HVDC orders in several years.
- High entry barriers in specialised magnet winding wire: utility and OEM approvals require demonstrated field performance accumulated over years, creating qualification cycles that cannot be accelerated, backed by a 45-year track record.
- Deep, sticky customer relationships - 97% of revenue from repeat business, longest-standing customer relationships of 40 years, and 120+ blue-chip OEM, domestic and global customers.
- India's largest exporter of magnet winding wires by export revenue, exporting exclusively to transformer companies across 24 countries, with long-standing relationships with global OEMs including Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Toshiba.
- Favourable mix: specialised magnet winding wires contribute about 75% of revenue, carrying meaningfully higher value addition than standard wires given manufacturing complexity.
- Back-to-back copper procurement against confirmed customer orders passes LME price and exchange-rate movements through to customers, so reported revenue moves with copper prices but absolute profitability does not.
- Scale and location advantage from Supa, which is strategically located closer to several customers and provides flexibility to serve domestic and international demand without trade-offs.
- Exclusive licence from HPW Metallwerk GmbH for globally patented Extruded PEEK high-performance wires, giving an early entry point into the 800V EV traction motor segment in India.
- Balance-sheet strength post-IPO: debt-to-equity reduced to 0.39 from 1.21, with debt repaid using IPO proceeds.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer concentration — The top 10 customers accounted for 51.15% of revenue in 2025-26 (the MD&A puts it at ~50% of operating revenue), so the loss or slowdown of a few OEM accounts would be material. Mitigation is diversification into high-growth sectors such as electric vehicles, deepening presence across 24 countries, and cross-selling specialised products to multiple divisions of existing customers to grow share of spend.
- Dependence on the power sector — The power sector contributed ~75% of operating revenue in 2025-26, tying results to grid, transmission and distribution capex cycles. The Company is targeting expansion into higher value-added segments beyond conventional power transformers, including EV traction motors and international markets.
- Raw material price volatility (copper and aluminium) — Copper is the primary raw material and is exposed to global LME price movements, which continued to influence reported revenue and percentage margin. The back-to-back order placement model - copper booked against a confirmed customer order with the supplier on the same day - passes LME price and exchange-rate variation to the client, so absolute profitability is insulated, but reported revenue and margin percentages still move with copper.
- Working capital intensity and negative operating cash flow — Significant growth has led to negative operating cash flows and stretched working capital cycles, and increased utilisation of working capital drove interest costs higher during the year. Management is shifting procurement from 100% advance payments to credit terms with copper suppliers to increase payable days and bring working capital days to sustainable levels - a change that has yet to play out.
- Foreign exchange exposure — Export revenues and imported machinery costs expose the Company to USD, EUR and SEK fluctuations, and depreciation of the rupee against the USD and Euro contributed to higher interest costs during the year. A formal foreign exchange risk management policy and forward hedging contracts are used to reduce the impact of adverse currency movements.
- Debt and interest cost — High borrowings had earlier affected the debt-to-equity position and interest costs. KSH used ₹225.98 Crore from IPO proceeds to repay long-term and short-term borrowings, improving the debt-to-equity ratio to 0.39 from 1.21 and reducing recurring finance costs, but the balance sheet remains exposed to growth-driven working capital borrowing.
- Supplier concentration and supply chain sustainability — The top 10 suppliers contributed approximately 98% of total raw material and component purchases, and the Company had no long-term agreements with raw material suppliers, relying instead on long-standing relationships. The BRSR materiality table flags Supply Chain Sustainability as a Risk, since manufacturing depends on a reliable supply of copper, aluminium, packaging materials and consumables.
- Quality, approval and regulatory compliance — Non-compliance with stringent customer, quality or regulatory requirements may lead to order cancellations, approval delays or licence-related issues - a serious exposure in a business where OEM qualification and pre-qualification cycles are long. Mitigation is international quality certifications including ISO and IATF, regular third-party audits and pre-qualification assessments by leading global OEM customers.
- Operational, technical and intellectual property risk — Manufacturing involves hazardous materials, process risks and specialised technical know-how. The Company addresses these through detailed employee safety manuals, periodic hazard assessments and strong IT security practices, and protects intellectual property through confidentiality clauses in employment contracts and registered trademarks. The BRSR separately identifies Safety/Health & Well-being and Labour/Employment Practices as material issues arising from shopfloor activities, machinery, electrical systems, material handling, chemical handling and contractor workforce engagement.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: 2025-26 was a major capacity expansion year built around the Supa facility, KSH International's fourth and largest plant, alongside its existing units at Taloja and Chakan (two) in Maharashtra. Phase I of Supa was completed at the end of September 2025, adding 12,000 MTPA of capacity across specialised and standard magnet winding wires, and a further 2,400 MTPA of specialised winding wire capacity was added at Supa during Q3 2025-26. Together with partial Phase II commissioning, total installed capacity rose from 29,045 MTPA to 43,445 MTPA as of March 31, 2026 - growth of 49.58% over the previous capacity base - which management describes as completing 48% of the Supa expansion. Phase II machinery has been ordered and, on completion by Q4 2026-27, is expected to take total installed capacity to 59,045 MTPA (described elsewhere in the report as approximately 59,000 metric tonnes); the Board's Report states the Company expects to reach 59,045 MT by March 2027 based on approved expansion plans and progress subsequent to the IPO. Ramp-up has been rapid: Supa achieved over 50% utilisation in its first three months of operations, while consolidated utilisation stood at 68% in Q3 2025-26 and 72% in Q4 2025-26, with blended utilisation at annual capacity of ~67% for 2025-26. Alongside capacity, the Company is investing in machinery at the Supa Facility and Unit 2, Chakan, in rooftop solar power generation at Supa (the rooftop solar plant was installed on May 02, 2026, after the Board noted a deferral of the deployment timeline from Fiscal 26 to Fiscal 27), and in a backward integration facility to convert internal scrap into green copper, with commissioning currently envisaged in H2 FY2027. IPO proceeds fund the machinery and rooftop solar objects, and the Audit Committee and Board reviewed the use of issue proceeds against the Monitoring Agency Report issued by CARE Ratings Limited, observing no deviation in the objects of the issue.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Copper is a complete pass-through and constitutes most of the cost base, so reported revenue moves with global copper prices while profitability does not; EBITDA per tonne is management's stated true measure of underlying performance.
- EBITDA per tonne improvement is attributed to three durable drivers: a higher value-added product mix with a greater share of large power transformer CTC and high-voltage applications, higher export volumes which carry a margin premium, and economies of scale.
- As Supa volumes ramp and utilisation improves from the 70% seen in Q4 FY2026, facility start-up costs will be absorbed and generate operational leverage.
- The global transformer market shows a meaningful supply-demand imbalance, with lead times for large power transformers extended considerably across major markets and OEMs including BHEL, CG Power, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Siemens and Bharat Bijlee reporting order backlogs stretching multiple years.
- India's transformer manufacturing capacity is estimated to rise from around 110 GVA to 300 GVA by 2027-28, with CG Power expanding 3.4 times to 85 GVA and Hitachi Energy and Siemens Energy doubling their footprints - creating downstream demand for specialised conductors and winding wires.
- Transmission capex in India is estimated at ₹9.1 Trillion over 2022-32, supporting a rising renewable share in the installed mix (from 34% to around 51% by 2029-30) and driving demand for transformers, reactors and specialised conductors.
- The grid's shift to 400 kV, 765 kV and higher-voltage systems, plus HVDC corridors for long-distance renewable evacuation, raises demand for technically advanced conductors such as CTC and insulated copper wires - segments with high entry barriers from precision manufacturing and long approval cycles.
- Demand is underpinned by the infrastructure supercycle: energy transition, AI data centres and global grid expansion; India added 52,537 MW of generation capacity until January 31, 2026 (including 39,657 MW renewable) taking installed capacity to 520.51 GW.
- The global magnet wire market is estimated at USD 36.66 Billion in 2025, expected to reach USD 38.51 Billion in 2026 and USD 49.27 Billion by 2031 (CAGR 5.05% during 2026-2031); India's magnet wire market is estimated to exceed USD 2.60 Billion by 2030.
- EV demand is an emerging driver: India's EV sales reached about 25.5 Lakh units in 2025-26, up 25.02% year-on-year, with the market estimated at USD 18.79 Billion in 2025 and USD 31.09 Billion in 2026.
- Policy support - Make in India, PM Gati Shakti, National Electricity Plan, Green Energy Corridors, Atmanirbhar Bharat, PLI schemes for white goods and autos, and BIS standards - is encouraging localisation and makes import substitution a meaningful opportunity for domestic players.
- Export demand may be influenced by geopolitical developments, tariffs, global industrial cycles, customer inventory adjustments, copper and aluminium price volatility, energy costs, logistics conditions and currency movements; companies with scale, cost discipline, working-capital management, raw-material pass-through and deeper customer relationships are expected to sustain momentum.
- Management notes the supply chain context has evolved: winding wire supply was tighter in 2024-25 but industry capacity has since caught up, and the broader bottleneck now lies more significantly in transformer capacity and other critical inputs.
- Commenced supplies for 37 HVDC transformer windings - the first domestic sourcing of HVDC winding wire in four years and KSH's first HVDC winding wire orders of the current renewable cycle in India, with several more wind and solar projects yet to be awarded to OEMs.
- Industry context cited by management: transformer manufacturers such as Hitachi, Siemens and CG Power are witnessing strong order books with capacities booked through 2029-30, and the sector carries strong order books of ₹700 Billion through 2026-27 - the Company does not disclose its own order-book value.

risks.note: The top 10 customers accounted for 51.15% of revenue in 2025-26 (the MD&A puts it at ~50% of operating revenue), so the loss or slowdown of a few OEM accounts would be material. Mitigation is diversification into high-growth sectors such as electric vehicles, deepening presence across 24 countries, and cross-selling specialised products to multiple divisions of existing customers to grow share of spend.

The power sector contributed ~75% of operating revenue in 2025-26, tying results to grid, transmission and distribution capex cycles. The Company is targeting expansion into higher value-added segments beyond conventional power transformers, including EV traction motors and international markets.

Copper is the primary raw material and is exposed to global LME price movements, which continued to influence reported revenue and percentage margin. The back-to-back order placement model - copper booked against a confirmed customer order with the supplier on the same day - passes LME price and exchange-rate variation to the client, so absolute profitability is insulated, but reported revenue and margin percentages still move with copper.
risks.risk: Raw material price volatility (copper and aluminium)

risks.note: Significant growth has led to negative operating cash flows and stretched working capital cycles, and increased utilisation of working capital drove interest costs higher during the year. Management is shifting procurement from 100% advance payments to credit terms with copper suppliers to increase payable days and bring working capital days to sustainable levels - a change that has yet to play out.
risks.risk: Working capital intensity and negative operating cash flow

risks.note: Export revenues and imported machinery costs expose the Company to USD, EUR and SEK fluctuations, and depreciation of the rupee against the USD and Euro contributed to higher interest costs during the year. A formal foreign exchange risk management policy and forward hedging contracts are used to reduce the impact of adverse currency movements.

High borrowings had earlier affected the debt-to-equity position and interest costs. KSH used ₹225.98 Crore from IPO proceeds to repay long-term and short-term borrowings, improving the debt-to-equity ratio to 0.39 from 1.21 and reducing recurring finance costs, but the balance sheet remains exposed to growth-driven working capital borrowing.

The top 10 suppliers contributed approximately 98% of total raw material and component purchases, and the Company had no long-term agreements with raw material suppliers, relying instead on long-standing relationships. The BRSR materiality table flags Supply Chain Sustainability as a Risk, since manufacturing depends on a reliable supply of copper, aluminium, packaging materials and consumables.
risks.risk: Supplier concentration and supply chain sustainability

risks.note: Non-compliance with stringent customer, quality or regulatory requirements may lead to order cancellations, approval delays or licence-related issues - a serious exposure in a business where OEM qualification and pre-qualification cycles are long. Mitigation is international quality certifications including ISO and IATF, regular third-party audits and pre-qualification assessments by leading global OEM customers.

Primary raw materials are copper and aluminium with enamel and paper as insulating materials, procured from a small supplier base (9-17 suppliers across periods) without long-term supplier agreements; top-10 suppliers account for 96.93%-98.91% of raw material cost. Manufacturing facilities are located close to Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Navi Mumbai) for logistics cost efficiency. Sales are largely make-to-order via purchase orders rather than long-term supply agreements, exposing the company to inventory/raw-material scheduling mismatches. overview.business_model: Manufactures and sells magnet winding wires — round enamelled copper/aluminium magnet winding wires, paper insulated rectangular copper/aluminium magnet winding wires, continuously transposed conductors, rectangular enamelled copper/aluminium magnet winding wires and bunched paper insulated copper magnet winding wires — from manufacturing units in and around Pune (Birdewadi/Chakan, Khalumbre and the Supa Facility) to manufacturers of capital goods such as transformers, motors, alternators and generators, selling both domestically and through exports (largest exporter of magnet winding wires from India by export revenues in Fiscal 2025). Revenue from operations was Rs 19,282.93 million in Fiscal 2025; the top 10 customers (including Al-Ahleia Switchgear Co., Bharat Bijlee Limited, CG Power and Industrial Solutions Limited, Emirates Transformer & Switchgear Limited, Georgia Transformer Corporation, Nidec Industrial Automation India Private Limited, Transformers & Rectifiers (India) Limited and Virginia Transformer Corporation) contributed 52.54% of Fiscal 2025 revenue from operations. Orders are typically placed on a make-to-order / specific purchase-order basis rather than long-term supply agreements.

one-line thesis: India's **CTC / magnet-winding-wire leader** — the copper conductor that goes inside every power transformer. Riding the same T&D super-cycle; mgmt is explicit that **transformer supply is THE bottleneck** and the winding-wire chain "will still have a lot more capacity to add to keep up." Record FY26 (rev +61%, PAT +62%), unit economics rising (EBITDA/ton ₹52.5k→₹67.6k), 5–7yr qualification moat, and a long import-substitution runway (India CTC demand ~40k→100–120k MT by 2030). Copper is pass-through → **track EBITDA/ton, not %margin.**

guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Volume growth FY27: ≥ last year's 21%** (full-year Supa capacity now available, was only partial in FY26).
- **EBITDA/ton: sustain ₹67,000–74,000** (mix- and export-dependent).
- **Exports: back toward ~40%** of revenue over a couple years (was ~30%, historically 40%).
- **Operating leverage:** kicks in *gradually after Q4 FY27* (new-capacity fixed costs absorbed first).
- **Cash flow:** FY26 operating CF negative (growth funding WC); fix via payables 25→30 days → better FY27 CF.
order book / demand model:
- No classic order book (make-to-order, 15–20 day turnaround); demand gated by **transformer-OEM ramp**.
- **Multi-year supply agreements** now being explored by large transformer clients for "predictability of supply" (same theme as Yash's 24–36mo blanket orders). KSH evaluating strategic/financial implications.
- **India CTC TAM:** FY25 ~40,000 MT → **FY27–28 ~70,000–75,000 MT** → **2030–32 ~100,000–120,000 MT**. ~1,000 MT/month was being *imported* on non-availability — now reversing.
capacity / expansion:
- **43,445 MT** at Mar-26 (≈65% specialized / 35% standard) → **~59,000 MT** after Supa Phase II (FY27; next tranche ~Q2 FY27). Peak util ~85%; new plant takes **2–3 yrs to ramp to 85%**.
- Optional **+10,000 MT** more (land/building/utilities ready at Supa) — decision pending demand.
- Q4 utilization ~70%.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **CTC (core):** >half of specialized; highest value-add; all exports are CTC to transformer cos on 4 continents.
- **Green copper backward integration** → H2 FY27 (cost efficiency).
- **PEEK insulated wires** (EV traction motors, 800V architecture): pilot end-Q2 FY27, meaningful 1.5–2 yrs out; EBITDA/ton ≈ CTC or higher. **Auto = 5–10% of the 59k MT capacity.**
- **Captive solar 4MW** (cost reduction).
margins & cost dynamics:
- Specialized EBITDA/ton ≈ **3x** standard. Mix (specialized vs standard, exports share, CTC share) is the swing factor — both grew, specialized faster.
- Weak rupee aids exports; **10% import duty + weak INR make imported CTC prohibitive** → domestic substitution.
capital allocation / balance sheet: - Sharply **deleveraged** (Debt/EBITDA 1.21→0.39x; most long-term debt cleared). WC 65–68 days, trending lower. IPO objects progressing (solar done; green copper in progress).
moat / competition:
- **5–7 year qualification barrier** for a new CTC entrant to reach 765kV/HVDC (PGCIL + each utility approves separately; entrants must start at 50/100 MVA and work up).
- 20-yr track record, integrated SPM lines (15–20 day turnaround), 120+ OEMs, >95% repeat.
- Transformer OEMs **unlikely to backward-integrate** CTC now (capacity available, complex continuous process needs order feed); globally none are backward-integrated.
risks & watch-items:
- Middle East shipment delays (~200–300 MT Q4 effect; rerouted/delivered in April) — temporary.
- Copper volatility distorts reported %margin optics (not EBITDA/ton).
- Negative operating cash flow in high-growth phase (improving via payables).
- Standard-wire growth outpacing specialized would dilute EBITDA/ton.
- New CTC capacity from existing qualified players (competitive intensity) — but qualification gates new entrants.
management quality / tone: - Clear, metrics-driven (EBITDA/ton framing), candid on cash flow and mix. Deleveraged aggressively. Conservative, demand-led capex.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The whole-chain capacity gap:** even if all announced transformer capacity lands in 3–5 yrs, the winding-wire chain "will still have a lot more capacity expansion to do" — a multi-year demand floor for KSH.
- Copper pass-through + value-addition matrix means **KSH's earnings are insulated from copper price** — only volume × EBITDA/ton matters.
- Import duty + weak INR are *structural* tailwinds turning a former import segment (~1,000 MT/mo) domestic.

cost_leadership.body: Backward integration is a stated aim of the manufacturing expansion: IPO objects include new machinery for expansion at the Supa Facility, a rooftop solar power plant at Supa, and new machinery at Unit 2 (Chakan, Pune), intended to improve supply chain resilience, reduce raw material costs and ensure consistent availability of high-quality copper rods, a critical input for magnet wire production. Manufacturing facilities are located close to Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Navi Mumbai) for logistics cost efficiency. Sales are largely make-to-order via purchase orders rather than long-term supply agreements, exposing the company to inventory/raw-material scheduling mismatches. Capex additions to plant and equipment were Rs 86.39 mn (FY23), Rs 258.32 mn (FY24), Rs 17.06 mn (FY25) and Rs 8.13 mn (Q1FY26), constituting 46.71%, 54.95%, 31.50% and 79.63% of total capital expenditure respectively.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Copper is a complete pass-through and constitutes most of the cost base, so reported revenue moves with global copper prices while profitability does not; EBITDA per tonne is management's stated true measure of underlying performance.
- EBITDA per tonne improvement is attributed to three durable drivers: a higher value-added product mix with a greater share of large power transformer CTC and high-voltage applications, higher export volumes which carry a margin premium, and economies of scale.
- As Supa volumes ramp and utilisation improves from the 70% seen in Q4 FY2026, facility start-up costs will be absorbed and generate operational leverage.
- The global transformer market shows a meaningful supply-demand imbalance, with lead times for large power transformers extended considerably across major markets and OEMs including BHEL, CG Power, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Siemens and Bharat Bijlee reporting order backlogs stretching multiple years.
- India's transformer manufacturing capacity is estimated to rise from around 110 GVA to 300 GVA by 2027-28, with CG Power expanding 3.4 times to 85 GVA and Hitachi Energy and Siemens Energy doubling their footprints - creating downstream demand for specialised conductors and winding wires.
- Transmission capex in India is estimated at ₹9.1 Trillion over 2022-32, supporting a rising renewable share in the installed mix (from 34% to around 51% by 2029-30) and driving demand for transformers, reactors and specialised conductors.
- The grid's shift to 400 kV, 765 kV and higher-voltage systems, plus HVDC corridors for long-distance renewable evacuation, raises demand for technically advanced conductors such as CTC and insulated copper wires - segments with high entry barriers from precision manufacturing and long approval cycles.
- Demand is underpinned by the infrastructure supercycle: energy transition, AI data centres and global grid expansion; India added 52,537 MW of generation capacity until January 31, 2026 (including 39,657 MW renewable) taking installed capacity to 520.51 GW.
- The global magnet wire market is estimated at USD 36.66 Billion in 2025, expected to reach USD 38.51 Billion in 2026 and USD 49.27 Billion by 2031 (CAGR 5.05% during 2026-2031); India's magnet wire market is estimated to exceed USD 2.60 Billion by 2030.
- EV demand is an emerging driver: India's EV sales reached about 25.5 Lakh units in 2025-26, up 25.02% year-on-year, with the market estimated at USD 18.79 Billion in 2025 and USD 31.09 Billion in 2026.
- Policy support - Make in India, PM Gati Shakti, National Electricity Plan, Green Energy Corridors, Atmanirbhar Bharat, PLI schemes for white goods and autos, and BIS standards - is encouraging localisation and makes import substitution a meaningful opportunity for domestic players.
- Export demand may be influenced by geopolitical developments, tariffs, global industrial cycles, customer inventory adjustments, copper and aluminium price volatility, energy costs, logistics conditions and currency movements; companies with scale, cost discipline, working-capital management, raw-material pass-through and deeper customer relationships are expected to sustain momentum.
- Management notes the supply chain context has evolved: winding wire supply was tighter in 2024-25 but industry capacity has since caught up, and the broader bottleneck now lies more significantly in transformer capacity and other critical inputs.
- Commenced supplies for 37 HVDC transformer windings - the first domestic sourcing of HVDC winding wire in four years and KSH's first HVDC winding wire orders of the current renewable cycle in India, with several more wind and solar projects yet to be awarded to OEMs.
- Industry context cited by management: transformer manufacturers such as Hitachi, Siemens and CG Power are witnessing strong order books with capacities booked through 2029-30, and the sector carries strong order books of ₹700 Billion through 2026-27 - the Company does not disclose its own order-book value.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: 2025-26 was a major capacity expansion year built around the Supa facility, KSH International's fourth and largest plant, alongside its existing units at Taloja and Chakan (two) in Maharashtra. Phase I of Supa was completed at the end of September 2025, adding 12,000 MTPA of capacity across specialised and standard magnet winding wires, and a further 2,400 MTPA of specialised winding wire capacity was added at Supa during Q3 2025-26. Together with partial Phase II commissioning, total installed capacity rose from 29,045 MTPA to 43,445 MTPA as of March 31, 2026 - growth of 49.58% over the previous capacity base - which management describes as completing 48% of the Supa expansion. Phase II machinery has been ordered and, on completion by Q4 2026-27, is expected to take total installed capacity to 59,045 MTPA (described elsewhere in the report as approximately 59,000 metric tonnes); the Board's Report states the Company expects to reach 59,045 MT by March 2027 based on approved expansion plans and progress subsequent to the IPO. Ramp-up has been rapid: Supa achieved over 50% utilisation in its first three months of operations, while consolidated utilisation stood at 68% in Q3 2025-26 and 72% in Q4 2025-26, with blended utilisation at annual capacity of ~67% for 2025-26. Alongside capacity, the Company is investing in machinery at the Supa Facility and Unit 2, Chakan, in rooftop solar power generation at Supa (the rooftop solar plant was installed on May 02, 2026, after the Board noted a deferral of the deployment timeline from Fiscal 26 to Fiscal 27), and in a backward integration facility to convert internal scrap into green copper, with commissioning currently envisaged in H2 FY2027. IPO proceeds fund the machinery and rooftop solar objects, and the Audit Committee and Board reviewed the use of issue proceeds against the Monitoring Agency Report issued by CARE Ratings Limited, observing no deviation in the objects of the issue.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: - Clear, metrics-driven (EBITDA/ton framing), candid on cash flow and mix. Deleveraged aggressively. Conservative, demand-led capex.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Only Indian supplier with approved products for HVDC transformers, and approved for all classes of power transformers - a position reinforced during the year by an award of 37 HVDC transformers, the first HVDC orders in several years.
- High entry barriers in specialised magnet winding wire: utility and OEM approvals require demonstrated field performance accumulated over years, creating qualification cycles that cannot be accelerated, backed by a 45-year track record.
- Deep, sticky customer relationships - 97% of revenue from repeat business, longest-standing customer relationships of 40 years, and 120+ blue-chip OEM, domestic and global customers.
- India's largest exporter of magnet winding wires by export revenue, exporting exclusively to transformer companies across 24 countries, with long-standing relationships with global OEMs including Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Toshiba.
- Favourable mix: specialised magnet winding wires contribute about 75% of revenue, carrying meaningfully higher value addition than standard wires given manufacturing complexity.
- Back-to-back copper procurement against confirmed customer orders passes LME price and exchange-rate movements through to customers, so reported revenue moves with copper prices but absolute profitability does not.
- Scale and location advantage from Supa, which is strategically located closer to several customers and provides flexibility to serve domestic and international demand without trade-offs.
- Exclusive licence from HPW Metallwerk GmbH for globally patented Extruded PEEK high-performance wires, giving an early entry point into the 800V EV traction motor segment in India.
- Balance-sheet strength post-IPO: debt-to-equity reduced to 0.39 from 1.21, with debt repaid using IPO proceeds.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- Middle East shipment delays (~200–300 MT Q4 effect; rerouted/delivered in April) — temporary.
- Copper volatility distorts reported %margin optics (not EBITDA/ton).
- Negative operating cash flow in high-growth phase (improving via payables).
- Standard-wire growth outpacing specialized would dilute EBITDA/ton.
- New CTC capacity from existing qualified players (competitive intensity) — but qualification gates new entrants.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **The whole-chain capacity gap:** even if all announced transformer capacity lands in 3–5 yrs, the winding-wire chain "will still have a lot more capacity expansion to do" — a multi-year demand floor for KSH.
- Copper pass-through + value-addition matrix means **KSH's earnings are insulated from copper price** — only volume × EBITDA/ton matters.
- Import duty + weak INR are *structural* tailwinds turning a former import segment (~1,000 MT/mo) domestic.

themes.title: Transformer & grid-component shortage
themes.need: Transformer makers are running flat-out at record order books even as core-capacity ramps land (ATLANTAELE 16k->63k MVA, Q1FY27 record order book INR3,117cr on record INR972cr quarterly inflow, Vadod now PGCIL 400kV-approved with a 765kV tech tie-up in final talks; TARIL toward 75k+ MVA, Q1FY27 UEOB INR6,630cr +26% YoY on a >INR1,000cr single-shot PGCIL Ultra-Mega order, though a Changodar-expansion air-pocket held Q1 revenue to +10%; SHILCTECH adding 220kV) yet the binding constraint is still everything INSIDE a transformer - CRGO core steel, CTC/winding wire (KSHINTL/BHAGYANGR), bushings/insulators (YASHHV; 18-24mo lead, ~95% RIP/OIP imported) and transformer oil (APARINDS); both OEMs are now backward-integrating to own the bottleneck (TARIL's INR900-1,000cr CRGO/CTC/bushing/pressboard programme). Capacity-gated supply is the repeated 'need of the hour' and is driving pricing power now, though both OEMs flagged ~60,000 MVA of new 400kV capacity landing industry-wide in 3-4 months as a 1-year-out overcapacity watch-item (neither sees pricing pressure yet).
themes.driver: PGCIL Ultra-Mega order conversion (TARIL's first >INR1,000cr single-shot award) + Vadod/Changodar capacity ramps; 400kV short-circuit tests and 765kV PGCIL approvals due by Q2FY27-end are the next re-rating triggers; TARIL's Changodar restart (Aug-2026) is the swing quarter for its own growth reacceleration.
